body: I read this post on LinkedIn from Dr. Daniel McKorley, and it just says everything I want to write in this article.
I feel everyone should learn to see potential.
I watched another video recently that talked about why Gen Z are always so "locked in" all the time. And I asked, why won't we be?

When the world keeps moving faster, the skills we went to school for no longer guarantee opportunities, and the opportunities that do exist keep getting harder to come by, you feel like you have to stay ready, stay prepared, stay sharp, just to keep up. It's no longer like the traditional "finish school, get a 9-5, and you are good to go."

And this shows up so clearly here in Ghana. You'll see job postings asking for 3, 5, sometimes 7 years of experience, when the majority of people applying are fresh graduates who just left school. So where exactly are they supposed to get that experience from if nobody is willing to give them the first chance?

Because let's be honest, most of the jobs we do today, school didn't teach us. We learned the real work on the job. Someone showed us. Someone corrected us. Someone gave us room to figure it out without writing us off the moment we got something wrong.

I'm not saying we shouldn't look for people who can do the job well. We should. But maybe the standard shouldn't only be "how many years have you done this?" Maybe it should also be, does this person want to learn? Do they show up with the right attitude? Are they willing to grow into the role? Because those qualities matter just as much, sometimes more, than a number on a CV.

I know how it feels when people don't see your potential. And I know it's not always as simple as someone just saying no. Sometimes people overdo it. They point out everything you're not, everything you lack, everything you haven't proven yet, until you stop seeing the potential in yourself too. That's the part that hurts the most. Not the rejection itself, but watching someone slowly lose hope in who they could become, simply because nobody paused long enough to look past what they didn't have yet.
So if you're ever in a position to give someone a chance, a job, a project, an opportunity, remember that someone once did the same for you.
"Skills can be developed. Attitude, character, and willingness to learn are much harder to manufacture." — Dr. Daniel McKorley

body: Since I came to the university, I have noticed something. How people act depends on the exposure they have had. This is not something I really saw back in high school.

In high school, you see people's actions and speech and rarely question them. The easy answer is that they are not mature yet, and none of us were, so it never feels like anything deeper. In university, you are around people old enough to have raised you or your siblings, yet you notice the same gaps in how they act and speak. "They are young" stops being a good enough answer. The real reason is exposure.

When I talk about exposure, I do not mean only the bad kind. Some people have had a good level of it. Others have not, and this matters more than most people realize, because communication depends on it. I made a post about this recently, saying that communication is a basic skill everyone should have. From a few sentences someone says, you should be able to tell where they are coming from and respond well. Eric Gugua broke this down well in a video once, showing how one careless statement undid an entire contract. That is what happens when someone has not been exposed to what a moment requires.
Exposure also shapes how we see and understand the world. My pastor, Pastor Enoch, preached about this on Standout, episode 10. You should really listen to it.

I remember wanting to move into a new stage of my life. God told me to go out and expose myself to it. You can sit in your room imagining everything you could do, but the people and opportunities you need are outside that room, not inside it. Nothing changes from thought alone.

As Christians, belief does not mean answers are simply handed to you. Let us take the example of scripture. I have read scripture I did not understand at the time, the Old Testament stories especially, only for it to return to me later, in a moment when I needed it exactly. If I had never read it in the first place, the Holy Spirit might not have had any other reference, and just like that, it would be gone. The same happens with things I come across online, even while working. I can be stuck on a concept for days, and something I saw weeks earlier, in a completely different context, quietly comes back and unlocks it.

People assume I watch movies just for fun, and I do, but they have shaped how I think and how I solve problems. I was once stuck on an idea for a client's ad. I had spent days trying to connect it to their audience, prayed about it, got frustrated, and put on a movie to clear my head. The answer was right there in the story. I picked it up, shaped it into the ad, and it worked. This has happened more times than I can count. It is never really about the movie. It is about what your mind already holds, ready to be drawn from. The exposure.

The same goes for how I dress. I spent years watching my family put outfits together, so I can do it too, whether I try to or not. People assume it comes from a love of fashion. I like to look good, yes, but I never enjoyed the process itself. I just cannot help doing it well, because I have been exposed to it constantly.
Last night I made a post that I learnt two things this year. Here are two of them.

The first is that visibility is currency. You cannot live in a country with a cost of living crisis,(and if you doubt that is real, look at the KFC incident), and still choose to stay invisible because you are shy or introverted. The real question is whether you want to win in your head or win in the world. Those are different games, and only one of them changes your life.

The second is that being enrolled in school does not mean you are educated. Book knowledge matters, but so does what my brother calls home wisdom, efie nyansa. People can often tell from how someone speaks or carries themselves whether certain things were ever modeled for them. It is not a matter of intelligence. It is a matter of exposure.

So it all comes down to one thing. Exposure is everything. If you want to grow in anything, buy the ticket, go to the conference, sit in the room with people already doing it. Build the connections. Just be there. Exposure does not come looking for you. You have to go and stand where it lives.

body: Last night my amazing, ever beautiful grandma came to town, and I had to go see her regardless, even though I had organised a tutorial session. Instead of cancelling on my study group, I carried them along to go meet her.

When we got there, we ate and talked for a while. Then Ishmael, one of my friends, said something like the advert on the TV wasn't right and he had a problem with it. Turns out it was an ad for a drug, and when the person got to the pharmacy, they just pointed at the drug and it was given to her. No test. No prescription. Just pointed. As creative as that was, it was also sending a strong and dangerous message: just point at what you think you need, and you'll get it.

We live in a country where we are trying to stop the idea of self medication, but these ads, one way or the other, try their possible best to show and express that message in order to gain views, and that's very bad. It's advertising working directly against the very thing we're trying to fight.

This isn't just a small habit we're talking about. I have had an encounter during my rounds in the hospital where a little boy's arm got amputated because of self medication. He hurt his arm playing ball, and instead of the parents taking him to the hospital, they decided to self medicate. It got worse. Eventually, they had to amputate. A simple hospital visit at the right time could have saved that arm.

Some of the symptoms we self medicate very commonly are things like headaches. We take para, but we forget it might not be the solution to the problem. Paracetamol simply helps reduce pain and fever; it doesn't treat what's actually causing the pain. Taking too much of it, or too often, can go a long way to destroy the liver, and that causes serious problems.

There are so many things going around that indirectly teach people to self medicate. You will see herbal drug sellers on TV and radio telling people that if they see these symptoms, they should buy this and that and it will heal them, instead of telling them to go get tested or seen by a doctor first. And the annoying part is we camouflage it with the warning, "If symptoms persist, visit a doctor." That's absurd. That line shouldn't be the last resort we run to after things have already gone wrong; it should be the first place we start.

If we truly want to win this fight against self medication, we have to start looking closely at the very things feeding it quietly in our homes every day, no matter how creative or entertaining the packaging looks. Because behind every catchy advert is a real person, a real risk, and sometimes a real loss that could have simply been prevented.

body: Growing up, my parents were busy people, so we had a lot of nannies pass through our home.
One day, one of them woke up and told my mom her money was missing from her bag. She said one of the children took it.
My mom, without even blinking, told her: "I didn't raise my children to be thieves. My children do not steal."
She didn't ask questions. She didn't call us to explain ourselves. She just said it the way you say your own name, no hesitation, no doubt.
I remember that day like it happened this morning. And it's the day I learned something that has stayed with me since: I can never be a thief. And none of my descendants ever will.

Not because someone taught me a lesson about honesty. But because my mother had already decided, deep down, who I was. She didn't need proof. She didn't need to investigate. It was already settled in her.
That's what conviction does. It doesn't argue. It doesn't defend itself. It just speaks.

And I think about that a lot, especially now. In work, in relationships, in the industry we build ourselves in. People will say things about you. Sometimes false things. Sometimes things that sting. And the true test isn't how loud you shout back to defend yourself.
The true test is whether the people who know you, the ones who have watched you closely, can say without hesitation, "That's not them," even before they ask a single question.
That's the kind of reputation worth building. Not the one you defend with words, but the one others defend for you, without thinking twice.
I don't know if my mom even remembers that day. But I do. And I know, one day, I will become the kind of person, the kind of brand, the kind of name, that someone else can vouch for that boldly.

body: Growing up, I didn't really know my native language that well. I'm Ewe, a proud one  by the way. And when I say I didn't know it that well, I mean I wasn't fluent. Wasn't really my fault though, my dad and brothers spoke English, I attended an international school, and my parents were busy, so I had little exposure to Ewe growing up. It was so bad my brother used to call what I spoke "pidgin Ewe." Broken Ewe. Such a meanie.

Fast forward to form 1 going into form 2. Due to one or two reasons this French teacher finds out I'm Ewe and decides to speak with me. We end up going back and forth, communicating, vibing basically. Then one day he looks at me and says something I will never, ever forget:
"You didn't learn the Ewe. You acquired it."

Till today that sentence lives rent free in my head. I wished my brother was there to hear it. The man went on and on about how my Anlo Ewe was amazing, and my head was swelling, because for someone whose Ewe had been called pidgin for years… ommddd.
But that comment planted something in me. Years later I'm still chewing on it: what's the actual difference between acquiring a language and learning one?
First thing that comes to mind is babies.

My sister Adepa. Every morning, my grandma would say she was communicating with the birds whenever she babbled her gibberish first thing in the morning. And me, on the other hand, genuinely thought babies had their own secret language only they understood. Weird, I know. But it might be true.
Turns out that babbling wasn't as random as I thought.

Babies are actually born able to hear every sound in every language, anywhere on earth. But somewhere in that first year, their brain starts tuning in to just the sounds that matter around them, and lets the rest fade, kind of like how you stop noticing background noise in a place you've lived in long enough. It's called perceptual narrowing.

A good example is Japanese and English. In English, "rock" and "lock" are two totally different words. In Japanese, that difference barely exists, it's more like one blended sound. At six months old, a Japanese baby and an American baby can both hear "rock" and "lock" as different sounds, no problem. But by around ten to twelve months, the Japanese baby's brain has quietly decided that distinction doesn't really matter, while the American baby keeps sharpening it because in English, it counts.

So with this whole idea of perceptual narrowing, I guess that's how babies born into bilingual or trilingual homes end up thriving with multiple languages so easily, way easier than an adult trying to learn a new one later in life. Their brains are just quietly narrowing in on all the languages around them at once, the same way they'd narrow in on just one.

So I guess that's what my teacher meant by acquisition. The Ewe seeped into my subconscious without me ever realizing it was happening. Nobody sat me down and taught me rules. It was just there, through years of being around it, until one day it came out of me sounding like home.

body: So I just finished season two of Avatar: The Last Airbender and some random, slightly weird thoughts came to me. Right?

You know how every nation in that show has its own rules. What you can do, what you can't do. During a solar eclipse, fire benders lose their power completely. During a great comet, it doubles. That's their biggest strength and their biggest weakness, and they guard that secret like their life depends on it. Because,well,it does.

But here's what caught me. Azula is the daughter of Fire Lord Ozai, and any time someone asks who she is, she doesn't stutter. She doesn't think about it. She just says it. I am Princess Azula. Blah blah blah, nation, bloodline, power, all in one breath. She has this confidence in who she is. And it made me wonder, if any of us got asked that same question right now, who are you, would we answer that fast? Or would we just stand there blinking.

It also brought back a memory. One of my favorite songs growing up is Heritage by Jadel. Every single morning my cousin played it on this small speaker, loud enough that whether I liked it or not, the song lived in my head all day. But I actually loved it. There's a line that goes, my name is Jadel, I come from Zion, I represent the Most High on earth, I speak in tongues, I heal the sick by thepower of Jesus in me. Turns out that's basically the Christian answer too. We're not really from here. We're from somewhere else.

I grew up in church. Sunday school, choir, quoting scripture on demand. I could have preached you a whole sermon on a random Tuesday afternoon. I did everything right on paper. But if I'm honest, back then it was all theory. I knew the words, I just hadn't felt the weight of them yet. So powers stayed exactly where cartoons left them, in my imagination, not in my actual life.
Now that I've grown, I see it differently. Power is real. And where you get yours depends on where you're really from.

I have a kingdom too. Mine doesn't fade with an eclipse or need a comet to work harder. It doesn't come and go depending on the weather. It stays, because it isn't pulled from the sky. It's the Spirit of God living in me.

So if I'm ever asked who I am, I already know my answer. My name is Kayla, I come from Zion, I represent the Most High on earth. My language is tongues. My power is the Holy Spirit in me, able to do everything Jesus did, and more.

So let me ask you  If someone asked you right now where you're from, what you speak, what kingdom you carry, what would you say?
Well Mine is Christ Jesus.

body: For the past two months, I haven't been actively working. Not in the sense that I did nothing. I was working, just not really working. I had a lot on my plate. But within those two months, I made a lot of observations. A lot of thoughts. A lot of thinking, the kind that sits with you long after the moment passes.

One of those thoughts hit me so hard, a thought about competition. And funny enough, I stumbled on a video by Victor Okafor, and he made me understand it better in a different light. Which is proof, honestly, that there's really nothing new under the sun.
Here's what I think.

There are three different types of people in every industry, when asked the questionwho is your Competition? The first are the ones who feel like they don't have any competition. They're good to go, nothing to worry about.The second are the ones who, when asked who their competition is, name the other people doing the same thing in their community, the other gym, the other podcast, the other brand. And then there's the third set. The people we're actually here to talk about. The people who understand competitive advantage.
Let me use Victor's scenario to explain it.

Say you own a gym. The gym's main goal is fitness, everything you do, every piece of content, every offer, exists to serve that one goal. The people who understand competitive advantage are the ones who, when asked about their competition, don't point down the street. They point to the alternative. Because when people aren't at the gym, they're still trying to get fit somehow. Slimming teas, most likely. Home workouts. Fad diets. Even surgery, for some weird reason(just saying). There are a hundred ways to chase the same goal, and your gym is only one of them.

So the real question isn't "who else has a gym near me?" It's "what do I do so people choose the gym over the slimming tea?" That's when you start creating content around it. That's when you start finding real solutions to a real problem. And that, funny enough, is how you become genuinely creative in your industry, not by outdoing the competition next door, but by out thinking the alternative.
That's the whole game, really. If you want to be great in your industry, that's the best place to start.

And after sitting with this thought, after stumbling on Victor's video, I went and checked it against every great person I could think of. Podcasts, business gurus, people who've genuinely made it in their space. Every single one of them works with this idea, whether they call it that or not. Not "who is my competition" in the way we're taught to ask it. But "who is offering the alternative to what I offer, and how do I out serve them."

Because there are so many ways to solve the same problem. If I want to get fit, I could join a gym, take slimming teas, get a trainer, try a diet, even consider surgery. Endless paths to the same goal. And it takes someone truly great to find the better solution and pull people toward it.

There's a lot I thought about in these two months, and that's what this new newsletter seriesKayla's Thoughts, Between Two Months'is going to hold. Every deep thought, every observation, everything sitting in between the noise. New issues drop every Monday and Friday, sometimes a Wednesday if the thought won't wait. Follow and subscribe to stay with me on this one.

body: Before the sun even thinks of rising, a young girl is already by her mother’s side, watching closely as she folds a kata, twists a dua, shapes an oríko, tightens an okwé isi, and smooths a pfundo. Different languages, different countries but the same small ring of cloth. The same little ritual. That simple head-pad is the first step in a long day, and it’s been that way for generations. This humble ring of cloth, though often unnoticed, is one of Africa’s most enduring innovations, shaping how women carry not only their loads but their stories, dignity, and identity.

For generations, the head pan has been part of the rhythm of African life. Long before factories produced aluminum and enamel basins, African women balanced woven baskets, calabashes, and clay pots on their heads. The modern head pan simply continued a tradition that had always existed a relationship between the body and the load, between posture and purpose. Young girls learn this skill early. They start with small bowls, slowly increasing the weight as their posture strengthens. Their mothers correct them gently, reminding them to keep their backs straight, to breathe evenly, and to allow their bodies to find a natural balance. By adolescence, the sight of a girl walking effortlessly with a full basin becomes routine, almost graceful.

But it’s not all effortless. Carrying heavy loads for years can affect the body. Some women develop back pain, neck strain, or tightness in their shoulders. Others become incredibly strong, but the strain is still real, even if they don’t show it. The head-pad helps that little ring of cloth sitting between the skull and the pan but the body still feels the weight eventually.

In some communities, the ability to carry a head pan used to say a lot about a girl’s readiness for marriage. If she could walk with a full basin without spilling a drop, it meant she was disciplined, hardworking, steady someone who could manage a home. It wasn’t just about beauty or age; it was about responsibility. Even today, especially in rural areas, that quiet symbolism still lingers. A woman balancing a load with confidence is admired for the same qualities people expect in marriage: strength, composure, and resilience.

But the story of the head pan is not complete without acknowledging the girls and women known as kayayei. Migrating mostly from the northern parts of Ghana to cities like Accra and Kumasi, they carry heavy loads for a living, moving through markets with quiet urgency. Their work is essential to the flow of the urban economy; without them, market activity would slow, and the movement of goods would become difficult. In many ways, they support the very backbone of these trading spaces.

But their lives are hard. They walk for hours with loads heavier than their bodies should ever carry. They work under the sun, in the rain, through insults, through exhaustion. Many sleep in unsafe places. Many earn so little. The same head pan that helps them survive also exposes them to danger, pain, and long-term health problems. Their work benefits society but society rarely protects them in return. Their resilience is powerful, but their situation is heartbreaking.(We can classify it as a necessary evil)

Still,across the continent, the symbolism of the head pan remains powerful. It is culture. It is identity. It is strength wrapped in silence. Whether it is called kata, dua, oríko, okwé isi, or pfundo, the head-pad beneath every load reminds us that even the strongest burdens rest on the smallest supports.

Different words, different landscapes, one shared rhythm: women walking with quiet grace, balancing their worlds with the elegance of those who have learned endurance not from books, but from life itself.

body: There is a tale that coconut trees came from the spirit of a man who sacrificed himself for his village during a season of drought.

They say long ago the land was dry. No river. No wells. People were collapsing from heat. Then one young man travelled to the edge of the sea and prayed to the spirits. He asked that his body would be used to bring water back to his people.
When he died they buried him near the shore.
And from his grave a tree grew tall strong with a head full of water.
That tree was the coconut tree.
So the elders say coconuts hold water because they came from a heart full of compassion.
And that is why coconut sellers are seen as keepers of coolness. People who carry refreshment from the ancestors to the living.
Just like Selassie.

Meet Selassie a young vibrant man located at Nogora Junction. He makes sure the people of Ho stay refreshed every single day. You can literally find him there almost any time. One thing that fascinates me is his ability to predict which coconut has plenty water and which has small water. Before he cuts it he will shake it look at you and say this one dier the water go be sweet oh. It is like a whole mini street ampe game. You guess he guesses then when he finally opens it you see who got it right. It is small things like this that make our culture feel alive.

When I first came to Ho his setup was just a wheelbarrow and a small stand. But with time I noticed how he kept improving. He rebuilt his shed he made his space more organised and that growth alone caught my eye. This is why I wanted to feature him.

Like I said in my earlier post mankind becomes valuable when mankind gives value to society. And Selassie is doing that in his own way. The sad part is that people still look down on his work. They call it dirty or work for the uneducated. Can you imagine. In 2025 people still think like that. Meanwhile this same coconut business is what helps him take care of his wife and child.

And honestly if more young graduates changed their mindset unemployment would reduce. Imagine a graduate with an entrepreneurial mindset (check out my earlier post on the difference between a business man and an entrepreneur (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/michaella-ashiadey-664854367_the-difference-between-a-businessman-and-activity-) even if he had just a supply of coconuts and a clean stand with proper packaging he could create something for himself instead of always blaming the government.

Coconut water itself has so many benefits. It rehydrates your body boosts electrolytes supports digestion and gives natural energy. So even the product he sells is real value not just random water on the roadside.
Selassie spoke about so many things. We could not even finish the interview because light went off. But his story is something I genuinely respect.
Watch the full coverage on YouTube.
https://youtu.be/xMR8-3-BZWo?si=7VZxcJsQa3h2GYUm

body: Like the baobab, our roots run deep and for my family,ours just happens to grow where the sea meets the sand.

For me, it all started with my dad, a fisherman. Most of who he is today came from the sea the early mornings, the smell of salt and smoke, and the rhythm of paddles cutting through calm water. That’s where his story began. And really, what better way to start The Baobab Chronicles than to return to that same shore where it all began for him?

In today’s world, a lot of people don’t see fishing as a serious job. Some even look down on it because it doesn’t come with office chairs, suits, or certificates. But spend one morning by the coast, and you’ll realize how powerful this life is. Many fishermen have built homes, raised families, and educated their children through this same work. My dad did. Our ancestors did. Fishing was their way of surviving, praying, and providing.

When I went to Sakumono Beach, I met a few uncles who have been fishing for years. They spoke with the kind of calm that only experience brings. They told me how they can read the sea the color of the water, the direction of the wind, even how the fish behave. It’s not luck; it’s understanding nature.

And it’s not just about the men. Women play a big part too. They may not go out to sea, but they handle the business selling, smoking, and trading fish. Without them, the whole system would collapse. In fact, some women run entire fish markets. But there are still traditions that guide everything. In some places, women who are menstruating can’t go near the canoes because it’s said to anger the sea gods. Whether you believe it or not, it’s part of the culture that still shapes daily life.

Fishing also has its own rhythm. Before heading out, fishermen pray or pour libation to ask for safety. Some days, no one goes fishing because those days are considered sacred. It’s not superstition; it’s respect. The sea gives life, and they know it can take it away too.

Beyond the culture, fishing feeds people in the most direct way. From the men who cast the nets to the women who sell the catch, and from the chop bars to the restaurants, fish keeps everything moving. One fisherman told me, “The sea may look empty, but it feeds more mouths than you can count.” That line stuck with me because it’s true.

Fishing might not make headlines, but it builds homes, keeps culture alive, and connects generations. So the next time you walk past a fisherman pulling his net or a woman smoking fish by the shore, remember this isn’t just a hustle. It’s heritage.
